utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, because of the potentially wide-ranging nature of these proceedings and the size of the Prosecution case, I have arranged for a number of the Prosecution team to be present. In order to my right, I have Susan Lamb, Michael Blaxill, Chester Stamp and Stefan Waespi and to my left is the case manager Ms. Adele Guzman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you very much and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. The Defence of General Galic is represented today by attorney Mara Pilipovic and by your leave, also the second member of my team, a colleague from Geneva who would like to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I see that the microphone is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The microphones are, but we still don't have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. I think I'm seeing it now in front of me. It's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, I just wished to introduce myself. I will act as co-counsel in this case. My name was given; I will be glad to repeat it. My name is Mr. Piletta-Zanin and I will assist Ms. Mara Pilipovic during this hearing and I believe at many others in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Allow me to welcome you most particularly because there's a great deal of work to do in this case. I think we can now begin. We have met here today to have a pre-trial conference as envisaged by Article 73 of the Rules of Procedure. As you are able to see, Judge Wald was not able to attend today, but you know well how much attention she attaches to our work and we will certainly share with her the discussions we have today so as to reach a decision by the Chamber which means we will not be able to rule today, we will just collect information and afterwards, the Chamber will render its rulings. I should like to tell you right away that in view of the number of issues that we need to address in the course of this conference, I have envisaged that we sit until 6.00 p.m. today and, if necessary, we will continue working tomorrow. So I am just alerting you to this possibility. This conference should be as fruitful as possible as we wish to allow the Chamber, which will be trying this case, to be able to begin the trial on December 3rd on the best possible conditions. We have always said that that should be the trial date. Saying that, I have not forgotten that the Defence has asked leave to appeal our decision regarding Defence motion that it would be necessary to review schedules 1 and 2 of the indictment dated the 10th of October 2001 as a modified indictment. A decision that we rendered on the 19th of October. I intend to organise the discussion around three topics, the points of agreement between the parties, the list of Prosecution witnesses, and the list of Prosecution documents. Naturally, we can wind up with an agenda item headed "other items" depending on what the points the parties wish to raise. That would be our fourth agenda item. With respect to the first item, agreements between the parties. The Prosecutor filed on the 26th of October 2001 a list of facts that are held to be undisputed by the parties. I will not conceal from you that we had hoped that your extensive discussions would result in a significantly longer list of points of agreement, longer and more significant ones, but we appreciate those that you have agreed upon and having read your pre-trial briefs, we wonder whether you may not already be ready to reach some other agreements. Specifically as regards General Galic and as regards the victims. Two points which we will elaborate upon: With respect to General Galic, I'm going to put a question to you and then ask each of you to respond. Do you agree that General Galic was appointed commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the 10th of September 1992? Perhaps I should begin if you don't mind, Mr. Prosecutor, with the Defence. Do you agree with this fact, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we enter into a discussion and respond to your question, I would like to underline that in view of the fact that there has been a request by the Defence to appeal your decision of the 10th of October, we consider this to be one of the crucial issues for the continued work of the Defence in this case, and it is our position that until a decision is made on this request by the Defence, that we cannot proceed with these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Pilipovic, I think that I have already said that we were going to hold this pre-trial conference regardless of your motion. The Chamber will decide what it decides, but in view of the elements that we have at our disposal now, we can have a pre-trial conference. If the Chamber should grant your appeal, there is some work that has already been done and there is more to be done but the Chamber wishes to continue the proceedings. To be fair and to treat equally the parties even after saying this, I would like to give Mr. Ierace a chance to respond to this point. What is your position, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as indicated in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief it is the contention of the Prosecution that General Galic was appointed the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the 10th of September 1992 and I note that at paragraph 2.30 of the Defence pre-trial brief, that is conceded. Perhaps I could add that at paragraph 3.9, Defence pre-trial brief makes clear that the Defence does not dispute the fact that General Galic was the commander in the relevant period. There is no specific agreement that the period of command ended on or about the 10th of August 1994. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ierace. The question that I put to you, it is still open but Madam Pilipovic raised a preliminary point, preliminary to all our work, that is whether we can hold this pre-trial conference in spite of the Defence request for leave to file an appeal. So it is this point that I should like you to comment on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position in relation to that is that proceedings at the moment are at the stage that the Appeals Chamber is considering the preliminary question of whether leave to appeal should be granted. That is no reason for these proceedings to not continue. In my submission, these proceedings should continue. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Pilipovic, have you anything to add on this point and to close the discussion on this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence still upholds its position that it is of essential importance for the Defence that a ruling be made on our request as it is based on the opinion that should such leave be granted, then it can object to the indictment. In such a situation, many decisive facts for the Defence would be contained in our objection to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Madam Pilipovic that you maintain your position, but are you ready to work today?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, the Defence also has a procedural, some procedural issues to raise to see whether we have the necessary conditions to hold this pre-trial conference now and with your permission, my co-counsel would present the position of the Defence regarding the Defence position at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these questions be raised under point four of our agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please remind us of that item?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first point is the points of agreement between the parties. We are now at the stage of the pre-trial conference. Then we have a list of witnesses of the Prosecutor and we must remember that we are still at the Prosecution stage, not the Defence case stage, and the third item is the list of documents of the Prosecutor, and the fourth would be questions that the parties might wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Your Honour? Thank you. The problem is the following: The measures that we have to undertake as the Defence has to be based on principles that we all have to respect here, those are the principles of justice which we all wish to respect first and foremost. And then, your servant included, has had knowledge on questions that you wish to obtain further information about and I was able to familiarise myself with that only a few hours ago. I personally am not familiar with the list of witnesses because I think there are some 100.000 documents. And in spite of my best efforts, Mr. President, I cannot provide an intelligent and logical response to your question when I practically don't know what we're going to talk about and it is not because I haven't done my work, because I wasn't -- but because I was not authorised to do it. And I think there is an essential element of respect for the principle of a fair trial is respect of time limits and, Your Honour, can this be undertaken because we simply haven't had the necessary information in time. Consequently, if we don't have that information, it seems to us to be difficult, if not absolutely impossible, to go further in cooperating which the Defence wishes to engage in. I don't know whether I was clear enough, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very clear, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Madam Registrar, do you have any information which would enable us to understand why it is that the Defence obtained the list of witnesses yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the day before. We were very belatedly informed and also the Prosecution brief was dated the 23rd of October of this year, 2001, which means that the imperative time limit of six weeks of Rule 61 ter which is the basic rule was not respected. I'm not going to say it was violated but it was not respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the documents that are filed are distributed the same day that they are filed. I will endeavour to find out what happened in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Registrar. When are you going to find out? That is my problem. I would like to know whether the documents were filed and when and served on the Defence because if the Defence tells me that they received the documents yesterday or the day before, then we certainly have a problem. It happens frequently that documents are placed in the little boxes, I don't know how you call them, but the Defence counsel doesn't come to pick them up. So I wish this to be confirmed. Have you any way of checking this, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will make a phone call right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do that and we'll wait for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, do you have the information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we have a statement from the Defence which says that, in English, [In English] On 29th November, 2001, in case Stanislav Galic and information confidential, the Prosecution filed list of witnesses pursuant to the Rule 65 ter. [Interpretation] It appears that the Defence was familiar with this list of witnesses far before yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not quite sure that I am able to read the date correctly, Your Honour. I am not sure I am reading the date correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we seem to have a problem with the date here. Perhaps it would be best to have a break now. We can't continue working like this without knowing exactly all the dates. The date I mentioned was mentioned in a document that you filed but you filed it on the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that I'm -- I am looking through the transcript and listening to you and if I read it correctly, it says the 29th of November, 2001. We know that the Defence is very efficient and it could hardly have filed a document on the 29th of November 2001 because that is not logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you, that was my fault, I apologise. I read that date out of context. What I wanted to say, but that is not going to help us much, is that on the 5th of November you filed a statement in which you mentioned a date, but that doesn't help very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I was saying, whether it is the 7th or the 8th, and we only received this the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, don't mention it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that even before we clarify this matter, there is something that I should like to say. I think that we have said repeatedly that we are now dealing with the pre-trial of the Prosecution and the intervention of the Defence is hardly anything at all, and when we come to the pre-trial conference of the Defence, in that case the Prosecutor will have almost nothing to do with that. As I said from the very beginning, we are not going to make any decisions today, we're simply trying to have some clarifications on documents that have already been filed, but those clarifications need to be made primarily for the Prosecution, not for the Defence. The Defence will not have much to do with the questions related to witnesses, their number, their identity, the arguments explaining why there are so many and things like that. So if you agree, I would suggest that for us to be able to make the best of the time, that we continue with this Pre-Trial Conference in this direction, that is, with clarification from the Prosecution with respect to its pre-trial brief, that is, its Pre-Trial Conference and then we'll have a break, maybe around 4.00. And then we may be able to clarify all these dates because in that way, we'll have had a certain period of work and then we'll see later. Would you agree with that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to respond, Your Honour, with the approval of my lead counsel, Ms. Pilipovic, I'm looking for the best logic like you, and we would like to avoid a problem when we get lost in dates. This could become quite monstrous, literally and technically to avoid that, and for us to be able to respond to all of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. points you are going to ask us about, it is absolutely necessary that the Defence be in a position to be able to do so. We were served less than 48 years [sic] ago, 5.504 pages. I apologise but I simply was not able to read through them so if I am expected to respond to my learned friends, you put me in a position of being a blind person surrounded by precipices, go straight ahead because that is where the door is. I can't do that because there are the precipices there too, and therefore, we cannot give you a position on matters that we are not familiar with because they were served on us only the day before yesterday. This is a principled issue in my opinion which I consider to be of fundamental importance, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can understand your position but we are working on the pre-trial management of this case now for at least two years. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are here today but I think -- the other attorney has been here for at least a year and the question that I was asking is a very simple one. I believe that we do not need to read the 5.000 pages. What I'm trying to make sure is that you, the parties, you submitted an agreement and after having read your pre-trial Defence brief I wondered whether there weren't other agreements because the Defence on several occasions -- well I'm not going to list the pages for you, but on several occasions say that I agree, but I contest that. You keep repeating that, I agree but I also object. What I'd like to know is whether it's possible to broaden the agreements; that is, the agreements were ready before. We don't need anything else now in order to deal with the question. That's what I want you to understand. Possibly I might find a compromise solution. I will ask you the question. If you are in a position to answer, then do. If you are not in a position to answer, then tell me, "That I am not in a position to answer because I did not read the 5.000 pages." I believe that that is reasonable, that is reasonable to ask you that because we have a great deal of work to do and we've got to get to it. Taking into account, taking account Rule 15 with Judge Wald not being here orders the continuation of this Pre-Trial Conference despite the motion requesting leave to appeal. We're going to do the work and the Chamber which comes after us will see what is the result of this request for authorisation and if the appeal is granted, the Chamber -- the next Chamber will see what the consequences are for having an additional Pre-Trial Conference. But one thing is to have a complete conference and the other one is to have one an additional one. Therefore, it is out of the question here to suspend this Pre-Trial Conference because of the appeal. The appeal will come afterwards. We will follow the course we have set out and if necessary, we will find at some type of crossroads. The other thing is that I was considering the first point on the agenda and that was the agreements. So I'm going to ask the question now. Let me ask the question of the Prosecutor: I thought that I would begin with the Defence because it has somewhat more to do with the Defence work, but the agreements have already been reached and I have them here. They've been reached. So the first question I want to ask you is, do you agree that General Galic was appointed the Sarajevo Corps Commander on the 10th of September 1992, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Commander, 10th of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I reply to your question, the Defence wishes to state that the Prosecution has submitted its stipulations regarding 26 points, 10 being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for a moment, if you could be direct. Answer the question directly. We already have the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree that he was appointed Sarajevo Romanija Corps Commander on the 10th of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is just one of the facts that we dispute, that that was that particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you are disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not have a document as to when General Galic was appointed Corps Commander. There is an allegation that the date in question is the 6th or the 7th or the 10th. Let me just quote the indictment of my colleagues, the date that is indicated in the indictment is the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. I think that we're going to find a way out of this. Do you have your pre-trial brief on page 1.331?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have my pre-trial brief; however, in my pre-trial brief it is quite complicated to locate the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 9 of your pre-trial brief, paragraph 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you write here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this brief, Your Honour, it is stated that on the 10th of September, 1992, General Stanislav Galic was appointed the Commander of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. What is it that you are contesting now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you now in view of the fact that the date of the 10th of September is contained in the pre-trial and we had some discussions as to whether the date in question was the 10th, the 6th or the 7th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, excuse me. We cannot work that way. We cannot work that way. You wrote that. We did our work. As I said, we're trying to broaden the agreement. I read, we read and you're reading that you wrote and you signed that that was the date and now you're telling us that it isn't the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The question I was asked was whether it was on the 7th of September, 1992. That was my question. I don't know what is stated in the transcript. I think that you asked me whether on the 7th of September, 1992, General Galic was appointed the Commander of the Corps, at least that is my note here. The question was whether he was appointed as the Corps Commander on the 7th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date of 10 September 1992 which you wrote in the brief is incorrect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no mistake in the pre-trial brief, however the question that I heard was whether he was appointed Corps Commander on the 7th of September, 1992, at least that was the interpretation that I received. That is in my note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, fine. I'm sure it's my fault. Having wasted this time, let me ask you the question again: Do you agree that General Galic was appointed Commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the 10th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where the error came from, but I think I always said the 10th but never mind. Excuse me, Ms. Pilipovic, but I just didn't understand. Pardon me. Perhaps there was an interpretation error. In my mind, I had the 10th of September. I don't think I ever said the 7th or another date. All right, fine. Thank you very much Now we have another point of agreement. The next question is: Do you agree that at the time of the appointment of General Galic as the Commander of that corps, all the units of the corps were assigned along the separation lines in and around Sarajevo and their responsibility was to defend those positions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. Could you tell us, please, so we could avoid any other technical problems the point that is being referred to, because the Tribunal noted it a little while ago in our pre-trial brief. Would that be possible, please? We're just wanting to check the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I don't think that is possible because we don't -- we didn't underscore that here, that is, the line, but all these indications came from your pre-trial brief. Perhaps the legal officer of the Tribunal has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only saying this in order to avoid problems like the one we just had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine, fine. These are the two points, point 35 on page 10 of your pre-trial brief, paragraph 2.35, 2.35. Do you agree? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the position of the Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ierace, do you agree with that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that places me in something of a dilemma for this reason: I'm not in a position to say -- to indicate agreement to the proposition that all of the units of the SRK were placed along the confrontation line in Sarajevo. However, I see what the Defence pre-trial brief contains, and in as far as its relevant to the trial, I have no dispute over that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we are taking into account your reservation. The question regarding the next possible point is: Do you agree that throughout the period covered by the indictment, the task of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was to defend the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that a question for the Prosecution, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me first ask the question of the Defence if you allow me to, but I'd like to see the paragraph because I didn't note it down. In any case, we didn't note the paragraphs. I don't know if you are in a position to answer the question. The question is: Do you agree that throughout the period relevant to the indictment, the task of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was the Defence of the separation lines which had been established? I think that you said that several times in your pre-trial brief. Perhaps we have an indication here, at least you say it once on page 7, paragraph 2.20. Do you have any doubts?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that first mission of justice is to have doubts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence sometimes have doubts perhaps contrary to the Prosecution and we have it only in respect of certain formulations, and I repeat that we are trying to be as specific and precise as possible. We are moving from one text to another. I apologise for the time that I'm taking, but I believe that this is work which is necessary, unfortunately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you have paragraph 2.20 in front of you. We also tried, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to be as specific as possible and noted that on several -- in several places, the Defence states that it accepts this. We have tried, whenever the Defence said that it agreed, to take that as an agreement between the parties. If one accepts that, there's no need to repeat the whole matter. Now, in -- with paragraph 2.20, we want to know whether you agree with what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can agree stating, however, Your Honour, that what is stated in 2.20 is broader than the definition you, yourself, gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. I stated that we had tried to suggest to you an agreement drawing from your brief. I am simply telling you the paragraph and that's where we got the idea from but if I can consider what we consider an agreement is not paragraph 2.20 but the formulation which the Chamber is suggesting to you from that point. And the proposed agreement is: Do you agree that throughout the period relevant to the indictment, the task of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was the Defence of the separation lines which had been established?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the wording is far too restrictive for the position of the Defence which has been expressed in point 2.20. Our position, our submission, Your Honour, which we will try to prove during the trial was that the separation lines were established after the initial conflict which was -- which were provoked by the Muslims at the beginning of March and which were established on the basis of ethnic supremacy in some municipalities of the city of Sarajevo so that the city was practically divided into a Muslim, a Serb and a Croat part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In any case, now we have your reaction and that is what we were interested in. Mr. Ierace, what is your reaction to the formulation of that point of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I agree, subject to the addition of two words to the proposition, so that it reads not "the task" of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was the defence of the separation lines, but rather, "one of the tasks". Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I have to tell you that the Chamber has not made the agreement -- has not reached the agreements. It was done at the suggestion that you might take that as way of broadening the agreements and we are going to suggest to you that the agreement be signed by both parties. So you will have the time to reflect on the matter again. Let me move to the next point possible of agreement. Do you agree that General Galic was the Corps Commander throughout the period relevant to the indictment? Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that there was no dispute in respect of this particular point that he was the Corps Commander throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Next point. Do you agree that throughout the period relevant to the indictment, the corps attacked military targets in and around Sarajevo which, of course, does not mean that it is alleged to have attacked only military targets, so I'm referring now to the military targets. Is there agreement about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are making progress, Your Honour, because the Defence instead of saying no to you is going to say yes, but that our formulation would stop after the words "military targets". We find the rest to be superfluous

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can go a few extra words and include "in and around Sarajevo," and agree with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take that as material to work with. We're going to finish with the points of possible agreement in respect of General Galic. In respect of the victims now, do you agree to consider that the conflict in the urban part of the city caused casualties within the civilian population and damage to civilian buildings? Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the trial, the Defence will try to establish the type of casualties and also the type Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of buildings that were damaged in the urban part of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Ms. Pilipovic, that's not what it's about. Do you agree that the conflict caused casualties among the civilian population and damage to the civilian population in the urban part of the city? We are not saying who the victims were and who caused them, whether it was the Serbs or the Muslims. The question is: Do you agree that there were casualties among the civilian population and damage to the civilian buildings? We are not specifying anything more than that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but in that situation, the Defence wishes to add that it did not only concern the urban part of the town but the entire territory of the city of Sarajevo, because Sarajevo is not only made of its urban part. It is made of at least seven different municipalities which encompass the population of that territory as a whole, and it is the submission of the Defence that this should concern the entire territory of the city of Sarajevo, that there were casualties and damages to the buildings in that entire territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in respect of Ms. Pilipovic's formulation or the Chamber's formulation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Chamber's formulation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So without adding what Ms. Pilipovic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no difficulty with the formulation proposed by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Another point of possible agreement in respect of the victims. Do you agree to consider that there were snipers and that the snipers caused civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we dispute this particular fact and we will call evidence to that effect during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask you the question a different way, Ms. Pilipovic. I am going to divide this point into two parts. I think I've understood your answer and I think that's what you need. Do you agree to consider that there were snipers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that simple question demonstrates the difficulties that we have. What is a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Ierace, what's your opinion in respect to that proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour allow me just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly I have no problem with the proposition, therefore, formally I agree with the proposition. I wonder whether there might be some misunderstanding on the part of my friends. I am attempting to locate a particular part of the Defence pre-trial brief that might assist Your Honour in achieving a greeter degree of agreement on this point. Your Honour, perhaps I could suggest that the Defence be referred to paragraph 4.11 of the Defence pre-trial brief. I wonder whether the Defence appreciates that the wording of Your Honour's proposition encompasses the notion that snipers -- encompasses the notion that sniping was not necessarily attributed to the SRK but rather embraces the notion of snipers in a general sense. Having regard to paragraph 4.11 of the Defence pre-trial brief, it would appear that the Defence indeed acknowledges that there were snipers intentionally operating against civilians in a general sense. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ierace. I think that that is why I did say it was general. The objection was raised and the question was asked about what is a sniper? I was going to invite the parties to reach an agreement on a definition because the definition is part of the Prosecutor's charges that the Prosecutor has a definition in respect of what is sniper is. But when one asks what is a sniper? perhaps we're not going to spend the whole trial or a large part of it trying to find a definition. We've got to have a definition, if possible, by agreement. Perhaps you have the transcript, you have the Chamber's suggestion. You know the various answers that were given. It might be a good starting point for you to reach a point of agreement, because it is true that as Mr. Ierace pointed out, even if the Defence used the notion without questioning it and so I do have some of the idea that there was something else that we could discuss but there is the notion which was used. In order to move forward, the notion here is that snipers, without it as being said that they were part of one side or the other, they were simply snipers. And the question was whether those snipers, defined generally, without stating where they were from or to which side they belonged, it's simply asking whether they had caused civilian casualties. That's the proposition and I will leave you with that. What I could ask you yet or to repeat is that this is the suggestion that the Chamber wanted to put forward, but I don't know if you are more imaginative and more -- have more fertile imaginations than the Chamber does in order to reach agreements. Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your honour. No one can be forced to do what is impossible, everybody knows that. What we can do is to speak with the Prosecution and review calmly in order to find out whether we can reach an agreement and I'm sure we can on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. What I wanted to do was give you a pretext for a meeting with the Prosecutor at least in order to discuss whether the points that we raised and I think some can, I think, can be used in order to broaden the agreements already reached. And if you have anything else, other points of agreement, that would be very good as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thank you for your cooperation. We will note your answers and I will ask you that as quickly as possible, you send to the Chamber a joint document, by that I mean a document signed both by the Defence and the Prosecution repeating all of the agreed points including those that were obtained here, and the others which might be obtained after your having spoken with one another. I think you understand that as quickly as possible, you are going to go back to the document, this document we have in front of us and replace it with another one with the agreements which to some extent we reached here and others which you might reach. Do you agree? Now, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will endeavour, after we receive the transcript from today's hearing, to analyse today's discussion and present its position subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me, Madam Pilipovic, to add other points too that you may be able to come across and on which you may be able to reach agreement. Do you agree with this procedure, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're now going to go on to our second agenda item and that is the list of Prosecution witnesses. We have another 20 minutes before 4.00. Allow me to say to you, Mr. Prosecutor, that you invested a considerable amount of effort which the Chamber appreciates very much; however, you have not made our task easy, both on account of the large number of witnesses that you intend to call, and also because there is a lack of synthesis in the presentation of your documents. Rule 65 ter of the Rules in fact requires that the counts and paragraphs that are relevant in the indictment should be indicated on which the witnesses will be testifying. You certainly did that. However, it isn't quite clear how many witnesses would come to testify on the same fact or the same subject or issue, and the Prosecutor has accustomed us to obtaining such a document which is very useful and that is the proof chart. This distinction is not immediately apparent, that is, between the witnesses who will come to present to the Chamber some general information, then witnesses of a particular fact or several particular facts, and expert witnesses. What I'm trying to say, there's a slight confusion, I apologise for using that term, it's the one that immediately occurred to me, that is expert witnesses, according to Rule 94 bis, and those who are going to come and authenticate documents. So we will need your assistance to try and clarify this fully respecting the strategy that you wish to adopt. Please correct me, Mr. Prosecutor, and also my colleague, but I have counted as various groups of witnesses, that is general witnesses, then witnesses on the role of General Galic, witnesses of particular facts, expert witnesses, and witnesses pursuant to Article 92 bis, and I must observe with respect to this point that the Defence agrees to only 10 witnesses. All these are Rule 92 bis witnesses, tend to enable the authentication of documents which the Prosecutor intends to use as Prosecution exhibits. We should like to review these different categories of witnesses so as to see whether it might be possible to shorten the duration indicated by the Prosecutor for the presentation of its case. So let us begin with what we have called general witnesses but just a moment, please. But before we address this chapter relating to the category of witnesses, it should be said that we are fully aware that you have grouped your witnesses into at least nine headings. I don't have here the French version, but the first chapter is terror; the second, command and control; the third - I don't know how to say that in French - on notice; the fourth, scheduled sniping incidents; the fifth, nonscheduled sniping incidents; the sixth, sniping generally; the seventh, scheduled shelling incidents; the eighth, nonscheduled shelling incidents; and ninth, shelling generally. If we add up several witnesses that are going to testify under these nine groups, and if we are not too strict mathematically, we are going to have 81 witnesses. As I was saying, we'll not be strict mathematically, but we will have the same witnesses coming to testify under several headings, as you know. Let us now undertake the analysis of the category that we defined as general witnesses. The Prosecutor intends to call a very large number of witnesses within this group, most of whom stayed in Sarajevo as members of UNPROFOR, 30 witnesses, or as United Nations monitors, 13 witnesses. Is it truly necessary to have all these witnesses be called to testify? Would it not be possible to make a selection? Some of them might have what one might call privileged information on what happened. We noted that some of those witnesses also appear under the category of those who may be able to provide information on the role of General Galic. Can we not there find a source of possible economy? So I have two questions. Is it really necessary to call all these witnesses that we described as general witnesses; and secondly, could we economize? That is, if I may, let me say that I think that the parties here, both the Prosecution and the Defence should be fully conscious of the fact that the Tribunal does not exist solely for this case and that we are using the resources of the International Community. It is paying all of us to be efficient and to be professional in our activities. And frequently, I have the impression - maybe I don't have the right to express my opinion - that the Tribunal is being transformed into a travel agency or an employment agency because, in my opinion, except in exceptional cases, there's no point in bringing a witness to testify for 15 minutes or half an hour except exceptionally. One must have a very good reason for this and that reason could be that this witness knows what he's going to tell us. It is a luxury to call a witness to appear for 15 minutes or half an hour in this Tribunal when we have witnesses who can provide the same information. So what I'm saying is that we must do everything we can to economize. If a witness is necessary for five minutes and if that is necessary for justice, he should come, that witness should come. But if what this witness can say can be said by other witnesses who are going to come here to testify for an hour, an hour and a half or two hours, then it should be done. You must bear in mind how much it costs the International Community to bring a witness here for such a short period of time if that witness is not absolutely necessary. So that was a digression on my part and I would like the parties to take this not as any kind of judgement regarding the conduct of the parties. It's simply that the Chamber would like to know what are the reasons explaining why it is necessary to have such a large number of witnesses and in some cases, could we not economize in terms of time and funds, et cetera. So Mr. Ierace, you have the floor. You are the master of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, in relation to the format in which the 65 ter witness material is provided, I should say that I gave careful consideration to adopting the Prosecution chart format but ultimately decided that the nature of this indictment did not lend itself readily to that format. This indictment is unusual in that ultimately all of the counts come down to the same crime base, and the format which I adopted, I think best reflected the structure of the indictment. Now, Your Honour has correctly noted that there is considerable overlap between most, overwhelmingly most of the 217 witnesses who the Prosecution proposes to call. That is no accident. In selecting witnesses, the Prosecution -- I should say, in selecting some groups of witnesses, the Prosecution has sought to maximize the number of witnesses who can testify to more than one part of the case. To put it simply, rather than call five witnesses to give evidence of five facts, it is preferable to call one witness who can give evidence of five facts or five areas. I say most because the witnesses who were selected for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to interrupt, Mr. Ierace, and I do apologise. But I see, for instance, that for the witnesses that are going to testify directly regarding terror, there are many who are testifying on several counts, there are some that will be testifying on four or five, there are many. But there are many witnesses who come solely to testify on Counts 1 and 6 when those same counts have been included for witnesses who are coming to testify on several issues. So I am underlining this because it is quite clear that there are many witnesses who will be testifying on chapters, 1, 5, 6, 7, and 9, many of them, 1, 6, 7, and 9, but there are also many witnesses who are only testifying on points 1 and 6. Why call witnesses who will be testifying on paragraphs 1 and 6 when there are many who are testifying on paragraphs 1 and 6 and many others at the same time? So that is my question. I can give you some names on -- for instance, Jeremy Bowen, Ismet Ceric, Dr. Jusuf Agiri [phoen] and there are others. These people that I have mentioned are testifying only on paragraph 1 and 6 and then you find a large number of people who are also going to testify on paragraphs 1 and 6 and then on 7, 8 and 9 or 5 and 9. So that is what I'm trying to understand, Mr. Ierace. Let me also say that there are witnesses for whom we have a summary and who are not on the list of witnesses. So we have some problems. For instance, the summary that you have on 1.568, page 1.568, and also the summary on page 1.556 and again 1.454, there are summaries there but you don't find those names on the list of witnesses. What Rule 65 ter says is a list of witnesses together with the summary of their statements, the estimated duration of their testimony, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and so on. Maybe I have caused a lot of noise, a lot of disturbance in the numerous questions that I have put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will check the witnesses, that is the 65 ter summaries which appear at those three pages and I will also give some consideration to the point that Your Honour has raised before then. I notice the time and that Your Honour said that we would adjourn around 4.00. Would it be convenient if we were to adjourn now so that I can look at that material and then respond after the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ierace, but there is a general question and that is: Do you really need the presence of all these witnesses, bearing in mind the fact that we should make the best of each and every witness who can talk about many things and avoid witnesses who will only be testifying a minor or one particular point which has already been covered by more general witnesses? So if a witness comes to testify on paragraphs 1, 6, 8, and 9, and you have quite a number of them, this combination 1, 6, 8, and 9 is repeated several times, this group of numbers. So my question is you have if you have a witness or several witnesses who are coming to testify on paragraphs 1, 6, 8, and 9, why bring witnesses who are coming to testify only on paragraphs 1 and 6? If there are already others that are covering this and I think that we are here at -- discussing things at a very general level. If we need to prove that there were victims, perhaps that's all we need to do. We have to know who the victims are, but we are not here to judge each and every murder or death, but come to the conclusion whether yes or no, people died, so maybe we should have the break now. You will have a chance, Mr. Ierace, to review the matter, perhaps, and Madam Registrar will also give us more precise information. Madam Registrar, do you already have some information to convey to us or are you going to see? No. Very well. Madam Registrar is going to look into this question of documents which reached you so late and we will see why because we have to know that, after all. So we are now going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, do you have the information that we asked for, the relevant information?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've been provided information from the Defence indicating that they received the witness list on the 2nd of November. This document was filed with the Registry on the 29th of October and notification was made on the 29th of October. For the exhibit list, I was notified by the Defence that they received it by mail in Belgrade on the 6th of November. This document was filed with the Registry on the 31st of October and notification was made on the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic. I don't think it's worth taking too much time about this, because we are going to continue our work, but yes, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The document dated 29th October containing the list of witnesses was received by the Defence through mail on the 2nd of November, 2001, in Belgrade. As for the list of exhibits which was filed by the Prosecution, it was picked up by the Defence on the 6th of November, 2001. It was in the locker, and I picked it up on the day when I arrived in The Hague around 13.30, half past one. The first document containing the list of witnesses I was only able to skim it through, and I provided our position to the Prosecutor on the 4th of November, that is regarding our position on the witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis. As regards the exhibits, we did not have enough time to study that particular list because we received it on Tuesday, on the 6th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Pilipovic. Thank you very much. Mr. Prosecutor, would you continue then, please, with the answer to the questions that I asked you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I understand Your Honours to be concerned that there are some witnesses who the Prosecution proposes to call and who are marked as giving evidence relevant to only one of the nine topics which are identified in the index to the 65 ter brief. Your Honour, where that is the case, there is often, if not always, a special reason. One of the names that you mentioned before the adjournment was the proposed witness Ismet Ceric. His name appears under the list -- within the list of witnesses nominated for the topic of terror. Dr. Ceric is in a unique position to give evidence about the effects of terror on the population of Sarajevo during the war since he was the head of psychiatry of the university medical centre during the war. He is uniquely placed to give expert evidence of the impact of what the Prosecution alleges to be a deliberate campaign of sniping and shelling of civilians. That's as much as I'll say about him at this stage but I simply wish to illustrate why it is that a witness who comes under only one heading is nevertheless a critical witness. Your Honours will note that there are the names of many other witnesses who appear under that heading of "Terror." Almost invariably that is because although they are witnesses primarily nominated under a different heading, they are nevertheless in a position to give evidence of their own experience in terms of experiencing terror as a citizen in Sarajevo and, therefore, that is material which is relevant to the first count. I appreciate that Your Honours are concerned that the witness list should be refined and reduced to the bare minimum, to the minimal sufficient number. I would like to respond to that concern with a proposal, and perhaps I can stay with the topic of terror to illustrate that proposal. As I've already said, there are a number of names on that list, but that is not the primary reason those witnesses are being called to give evidence. The primary reason for many of them is that they are a witness to a scheduled sniping incident or a scheduled shelling incident. It may well be that having heard evidence from the first two or three of the witnesses whose names appear on the "Terror" list, and in particular, their evidence in relation to terror, that the Trial Chamber will, in effect, take judicial notice of what I would submit is a fact, that if a civilian is living in an urban setting where they are at danger of being sniped or shot or their loved ones are in danger of being sniped and shot or their friends, that that will engender in them, if you like, as a matter of human nature, a sense of terror. At that point, further evidence from these various witnesses to that effect could stop. Another area of the Prosecution brief that may be examined in a similar light is the topic of what I might call the pre-indictment history. Your Honours will note that in the 65 ter summaries, there recurs a subheading "Pre-indictment History." There are a number of witnesses who, in their statements, recount events which occurred between the commencement of the armed conflict in around April or May of 1992 and the beginning of the indictment period in early September 1992. To an extent there is relevance in that material, the pre-trial brief articulates that it is the Prosecution's contention that General Galic took over a pre-existing campaign of sniping and shelling. The Prosecution contends that the confrontation lines were essentially established before General Galic assumed command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It is, I would readily concede, unnecessary for every witness who is in a position to do so to give evidence of that period. So again, once that evidence is given the first time, perhaps the second, then the position of the Prosecution would be secure in terms of not having to lead further evidence under that topic. Perhaps that doesn't assist the Trial Chamber in reducing the overall number of witnesses. From that perspective, there are two possible areas where witnesses may be shed. The first such grouping is what internally the Prosecution refers to as "overview witnesses," that is, witnesses who are able to give an overview of the events of the indictment period, and in some cases, the pre-indictment period. The mayor of Sarajevo at the time is one such witness. I do not suggest that that individual should not be a witness, but to give another example, there is a witness who represents the water authority, who is able, in short evidence, to give a summary of the periods of time that the water was not available to the civilians of Sarajevo. I should add that the relevance of that evidence is not to the effect that the SRK, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, or General Galic sought out to cut off the water, but rather, it was, amongst other factors, the lack of utilities within the home which forced civilians out of the relative safety of the home on a daily basis and onto the street; in other words, to obtain water, fuel for warmth and cooking and so on. Those -- that sort of evidence is ripe to be treated by way of 92 bis, Rule 92 bis, and indeed a number of the witnesses that we propose to be treated that way were such witnesses. The second area that may lend itself to some reduction is the internationals, for lack of a better term, that is, individuals who were in Sarajevo at some point during the indictment period, but who originated from outside. They were non-residents. They were often there in their work capacity as members of UNPROFOR, UNMO, UNHCR, and other agencies. Their evidence is valuable, and Your Honours will note that there is a relatively large number of them. I hasten to add that the reason for that, in a large part, is the length of the indictment period. Typically such witnesses were not in Sarajevo for the entire 22 months. Indeed, typically they were there for three to six months. Nevertheless, in that period which they were present, they witnessed events which are important to the Prosecution case. Perhaps I should say at this juncture that essentially the Prosecution case is a circumstantial one. It's one that must be built with a multitude of small components of evidence in order to lead the Trial Chamber, in the Prosecution case, to the conclusion which the Prosecution proposes. So Your Honours, I'm saying that although there appears to be on the face of it a large number of such witnesses, given the length of the indictment period and the short periods which these witnesses were present, that is the reason that there are so many. Nevertheless, it may be that we could reduce some of the witnesses from that category. I hasten to add though that we have exercised a lot of care and put a lot of thought into this final list. Whilst it may seem on the face of it that there is perhaps -- there are perhaps too many, when one has regard to the rationale for each witness, in fact, I don't think it is the case. Therefore, if we were to reduce the list of our own volition, I would not anticipate a dramatic reduction in the overall number of witnesses. I would rather submit that the overall length of the Prosecution case would be better reduced by having regard to the topics under which so many of the witnesses will give evidence, such as terror and such as the pre-indictment period. If I might refer to another of the names that Your Honours mentioned, Your Honour mentioned before the break that of Dr. Hadzir. It appears that Dr. Hadzir's name only appears on the list of terror and perhaps that is an oversight on the part of the Prosecution. Dr. Hazir was the hospital which came to be know as the Srbinje Hospital. It was set up during the armed conflict and quickly swelled in numbers of medical staff and in numbers of patients to a point where it operated as a minor general hospital treating hundreds of civilian patients on a regular basis. Dobrinje was also a particular theater of the war which warrants some special attention. Your Honours will note that a number of the shelling and sniping incidents occurred in Dobrinja and I think that the Trial Chamber will benefit from the testimony of Dr. Hadzir who is uniquely placed to comment on not only the extent of civilian casualties in that that area that he treated through his hospital, and in particular children, but also because he was forced to live in the area, he could not always safely return to his home in a different part of Sarajevo. He's able to give first-hand evidence as to the impact, from his own observation, of the shelling campaign in Dobrinja. So Your Honours, that's what I propose as a -- perhaps a preferred way from the Prosecution perspective of reducing the length of the Prosecution case. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ierace. I understand your reasons in respect of the examples we took, but I do note, you know when I talked about headings 1 and 6, I'm talking about the list of witnesses for terror, and snipers in general. But if we have witnesses who come who are going to testify only in respect of headings 1 and 6, we could see that there is 31 witnesses who, in addition to testifying to other headings will also be testifying about headings 1 and 6. You explained to us that it's a psychiatrist who is going to check on the effects of terror - might be a medicine - who observed people who were ill. All right, but if we have this testimony already, why do we have to have 31 other witnesses to speak about it even if it's from another perspective because I think that it really isn't necessary for the case to supplement every perspective possible to bring in every possible person, any person who might be in a position to testify about heading 1 and 6. What I was thinking is -- the Chamber, you see, needs to have your position and to understand it very well because, as you know, the Chamber can reduce the number of witnesses. Yes, it's easy to say that, but the Chamber, I think, can only do that according to its own discretion. And they could say, "I don't like this one. I don't like that number. I'm going to cut it out." But if the Chamber is being to reduce the number, it has to have good reasons for doing so and one must take into account the fact that the -- the principle is that the parties build their cases and that principle must be respected. As you know, we've got to strike a balance in the Rules, that the Chamber can reduce the number of witnesses with reasonable criterion but at the same time, it can set up a pool of reserve witnesses in which the parties could then use to say that "I finished presenting my case," whether it's the Prosecution or the Defence, "And I realise, Your Honours, that for this and that reason, for this and that witness on my reserve list, I'm going to need that person." You can always come back and try to get to the very essential witnesses of the cases. I can share my vision of the case with you. We have witnesses, to some extent, excuse the expression, who are really kind of umbrellas for the whole case. We could mention for example the witnesses you have just mentioned, the 30 witnesses from UNPROFOR, the 13 United Nations monitors and as you say, it's because they did not remain throughout the time covered by the indictment, but if you add up 1, 2, 3 and 4, perhaps you would then have a set of witnesses that could cover the entire period relevant to the indictment, and that would be kind of a general umbrella. Subsequently, if you need witnesses for each incident for specific facts in that case, it isn't necessary -- my way of looking at this case, perhaps it might not be necessary, to bring in 60 witnesses for the shelling incidents. Perhaps if you realise that several incidents were spread out from 1992 and then 1993, 1994, in 1992, you -- for 1992 you've got five witnesses, in two incidents; for 1993, 32 witnesses, there were more incidents; and for 1994, you've got 22 witnesses. If you have a kind of an umbrella witness for the whole case, you might not need to call in so many witnesses and one could also see that in respect of each incident. For instance, one could have the market Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. incident where there were many witnesses that you've mentioned. For that incident, you might have umbrella witnesses, those who observed things in hospitals, funeral directors, people that would cover the entire incident and then for the specific incidents within the umbrella case, you'd bring in another witness. So perhaps we could organise the witness list according to that logic; that is, that there are general witnesses for the whole thing, that is umbrella witnesses, and then you could have to go into all the details for several incidents. So one could say that for each incident there would be one witness for each incident, possibly two if the incident is important enough and one witness might not have all the information. That would be a way of enormously reducing the number of witnesses, one strengthen the umbrella witnesses and cut down significantly the witnesses to specific incidents. What do you think about that, Mr. Ierace? And this has to do with the comment that I made because it is true that there are witnesses -- let's go back to headings 1 and 6. Yes, there are witnesses three or four at least, who will come only to testify to those two headings, 1 and 6, but then afterwards, there are at least 31 witnesses for whom headings 1 and 6, along with 2, 8 or 9, are also going to be testifying; that is, witnesses testifying about other headings, that is the 31, but also testifying about 1 and 6. So that's the kind of philosophy that can be used in such a way that one would find a witness that would cover the largest amount of things possible and thus avoid bringing in a witness who would testify only about a specific point unless, as I said - and I do emphasise this point - unless that witness who would come to witness only about a specific point was called. If he were to testify between 15 minutes or 30 or 45 minutes, we should be able to do everything we can to avoid that kind. If another witness is going to come in and testify, we don't need to bring in a witness only for so short a time and for so specific a point. Do you understand what I mean, Mr. Ierace? Let me hear what your reaction is. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honours, please forgive me for responding in a way that perhaps follows on from my previous submissions. Could I firstly say this: Your Honour has again referred to the list of witnesses for terror, that is, point 1. Apart from Dr. Ceric, I think without exception -- I'll put it this way: If we were to take the names of all of the remaining "Terror" witnesses from that list, then the overall number of witnesses to be called would be barely reduced. In other words, with the exception of Dr. Ceric, almost without exception, every other name on that list is of a witness who is primarily giving evidence under a different topic. If I could approach it a different way. In the comments which are contained on the first page of the Prosecutor's list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 65 ter, and I refer specifically to page 1.596, Your Honours will see the number of witnesses under each of the relevant categories for each of the counts. It might be helpful if I was to indicate the primary categories, and perhaps in doing it that way, I can make my point. Under Counts 2 to 4, the number of witnesses in relation to scheduling sniping incidents is identified as 63. So of the 217 overall witnesses, 63 are giving evidence - that is almost a third - because they are relevant to scheduled sniping incidents. I can tell Your Honours, if I just refer further to the scheduled sniping incidents, that of the 26 scheduled sniping incidents, approximately in respect of 18 there are only two witnesses per incident, and in some of those cases, there is one civilian witness and a police officer or the like who carried out an investigation. There are another four or five incidents where there is only one witness. Further, in relation to the sniping, the Trial Chamber will have the benefit of the video, the DVD, so that the witness -- the evidence given by those witnesses, I anticipate, will be very short because it will be, in effect, supplemented by the video. I move further down the list for the witnesses, the number of witnesses under counts 5 to 7, and in particular witnesses in relation to scheduled shelling incidents, 71. So if one combines that figure of 71 with the figure of 63, one has 134. Over half the witnesses have to be here anyway because they are to give evidence in relation to the scheduled incidents. They are what perhaps I could refer to as primary witnesses or witnesses who give evidence to primary aspects of the Prosecution case. In a similar category, I take Your Honours to witnesses in relation to notice to the accused of the shelling of civilians, 34; and witnesses in relation to the accused's command and control, 37. There is some overlap between those two groups of 34 and 37. They are the UNMOs, UNPROFORs and the like. But if you add all those numbers together, you in effect have the Prosecution witness list. It happens that the witnesses who are coming here anyway to give evidence as to scheduled sniping incidents are also able to recount observations and awareness of a multitude of unscheduled sniping incidents, unscheduled shelling incidents, and give evidence generally about the sniping and the shelling. The Trial Chamber will benefit from that material because it will give the Trial Chamber a sense of the scale of the magnitude of the campaign, and I emphasise the word "campaign." Our point is essentially this, that if there is to be a reduction of witnesses of any significance, then they have to come off those primary lists. And my illustration of that point is that if you took up all but one of the names on the "Terror" list, it would barely impact, if at all, on the overall number of witnesses. They are witnesses who are coming anyway who are in a position to talk about terror. There are two witnesses who, in effect, talk directly on terror, Dr. Ceric, a psychiatrist who was there at the time, and an expert witness on terror still to come. The same could be said of the witnesses who speak about unscheduled shelling, unscheduled sniping, and sniping and shelling generally. If those four lists were wiped out, there would be little impact on the number of witnesses. So the focus has to be on those primary lists. And when one looks at those primary lists, it's difficult to see where the cuts should be. That is the difficulty that I have in proposing how the Prosecution could significantly reduce that list. But I hasten to add, I think that we can reduce the amount of time that each of the witnesses is in the witness box. And further - can I say this, Your Honours? - the Prosecution has made a proposal in relation to 92 bis. The response from the Defence has been, in effect, to reject it. I think there are only two or three witnesses who the Defence is prepared to accept as 92 bis witnesses. I think that there is a lot of room for moving witnesses off the viva voce list onto 92 bis if there is a more receptive approach by the Defence. In particular, a lot of the overview witnesses, I think, could be moved into that area. There are two names that Your Honours mentioned before the adjournment who clearly should be in that list. One was a nurse who was in a position to authenticate medical records documents, and the other was an employee of the television station who can authenticate videos. They should clearly be 92 bis. The Defence has made clear in its response to our proposal for 92 bis witnesses that they have concerns about the quality of the medical records. In particular, they say they want some evidence as to the manner in which the records were taken. We're happy to provide that, to find a witness who will testify as to what the procedure was. The Defence also articulates a concern that the records are not uniformly legible. There's nothing the Prosecution can do about that. The Prosecution has taken further investigative steps to get better copies without success. That's something the Prosecution has to weigh. It's a factor to be taken into account in assessing the relevant issues. That is not a reason, in my submission, to not accept the documents under 92 bis. Perhaps when there is a statement as to the manner in which the records were taken, the Defence could review its stance in relation to the receiving into evidence of the records themselves. I say these things as an example of how the Prosecution case can be reduced without necessarily drastically reducing the number of witnesses. The Prosecution is also hopeful that many of those witnesses can give -- the crime base witnesses can give evidence by video from Sarajevo to avoid a large number of witnesses being transported to The Hague. Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ierace, let us try and analyse these things, but regarding Rule 92 bis, it is true that the Defence is entitled not to agree. But it is also true that this will be a suggestion that this Chamber will pass on to the Chamber that will try the case, but they also have to say why they don't accept and after the reasons are given by the Defence, it is quite possible to limit, to hold the Defence to the reasons that they gave for not agreeing. So it's not an open-ended right to cross-examine the witnesses, but only based on the reasons that the Defence is has given for not accepting and all this can speed things up. Perhaps there will come a point in time when the Chamber will say to the Defence, "Fine, you don't accept a Rule 92 bis, but why?" And then the Defence will say for such and such a reason. And then the Chamber will say, "Fine, you will be able to cross-examine on the points of disagreement." But I cannot impose that upon you, but I would do it if I was there, because that is absolutely fair and reasonable to do that. And I also take advantage of the moment to say the same thing with respect to expert witnesses but I will come to that so I don't want to mix things up. The second category of witnesses were the witnesses on the role of General Galic. As I noted a moment ago, the number of general witnesses appear to have information on the role of General Galic, in particular, specifically on the information communicated to him regarding shelling and sniping. So my question to Mr. Ierace is: Isn't there also an important margin for saving time and calling witnesses who were directly related to General Galic who, who had direct contact with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not necessarily an efficient and comprehensive way for the Prosecution to present its evidence in relation to the role of General Galic because there were UNPROFOR officers at a certain level that communicated with General Galic, there were others under that level who communicated with his senior subordinates and the evidence will demonstrate that what was communicated to his senior subordinates as a matter of the organisation of the SRK would make its way up that course to the accused. So in order to present all of the relevant evidence as to what was communicated to General Galic, one must go beyond those senior officers who had direct communication with him to the junior officers who communicated at their respective level within the accused's chain of command. Having said that, there are a number of Prosecution witnesses who were relatively down the UNPROFOR and UNMO chain of command who the Prosecution proposes to call, but then their evidence often is particularly relevant because of observations they have made of artillery units. For instance, in some cases they have communicated with artillery officers or viewed artillery units firing into civilian areas or had important conversation with -- conversations with lower-ranking but relevant echelons of the accused's staff. Your Honours, it may seem as if I am thwarting your attempts to reduce the witness list. It's simply that I can assure that you that a lot of thought went into this list before we conveyed it to the Registry and I can also assure you that this list is far less than the number of witnesses who were available to us. And, if you like, there has been a cull of witnesses within the OTP before we transmitted this list.
