The areas that I have identified are the only areas that I could responsibly as the trial attorney propose for further reduction. Could I say one more -- make one further observation as to why it may seem that the list is unnecessarily large? And that is that we are talking not only about a 22-month indictment period, not only about a circumstantial case, but as well, we are talking about criminality which, by it's nature, did not lend itself easily to the identification of the perpetrators. Sniping by its very nature involves the shooter discharging a weapon from a concealed or partly concealed position in an urban setting where the confrontation line often involved the sides being only metres apart. In other words, there is something about the character of this case, about its very nature which requires, in my view, the Prosecution to lead more evidence than one would expect in a different trial where, perhaps, the important events occurred within a period of weeks at one particular place and where identification was not such a critical issue. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ierace. We understand the specificity of the case, but we will have several incidents either of sniping or shelling. The schedules that you filed regarding witnesses for specific events refer to 27 facts concerning victims of snipers and 5 incidents of shelling. Regarding the victims of snipers, the Prosecutor plans to call 63 witnesses for incidents appearing in the schedules, but 41 witnesses for incidents which are not specified. The Prosecutor also plans to have 120 witnesses for sniping incidents in general. We feel that in view of the information at the disposal of the Chamber, that can hardly be acceptable. You have already understood, Mr. Ierace, that the Chamber is endeavouring to reduce the number and you are trying to maintain the number. What the Chamber would like to have from you, to hear from you is the reasons why you believe because, as I have said, the Chamber can reduce the number, but it must have reasons for doing so and that is why we wanted to devote this hearing to discussing your reasons. Could you explain why you would need so many witnesses on nonspecific incidents in the schedules? It is true and this is also connected to the question that is going to be appealed by the Defence, that the Chamber has admitted certain facts which might corroborate certain standard behaviours, but if I consider these facts together, that is, the sniping and the shelling, I see that for 27 incidents in 1992, you call 5 witnesses; for 1993, 32; for 1994, 22. And if we look at the second schedule, we have at least 60 witnesses. If I go back to what I was saying about these umbrella witnesses and specific witnesses, we have a total of almost 120 witnesses for all these incidents. It is true that for each incident, you have one witness, for some you have four, for some again you have three and for other shelling incidents, you have 23 or 10 or 11 witnesses. So regarding the sniping incidents, if one says we have the umbrella witness, we might have one or two additional witnesses but as a rule, to have one witness for each incident, wouldn't that be sufficient? And we could cut almost by half the number. Do you, again I'm asking you, need so many witnesses for non-specified incidents in the annex, in the schedule? It is true that I am trying to reduce the number, you are trying to maintain your number but I say again we would like to hear your reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, and perhaps as an example I will start with schedule sniping incident number 4 where the victim was [redacted]. I will explain why it is that we are calling three witnesses in relation to that incident rather than one. [redacted] was shot and wounded whilst attending -- whilst in his vegetable garden outside his home. He lost -- he became semi-conscious after he was shot Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and lay on the ground until his wife and daughter and another relative who were in his home noticed that he had not returned to the home and went looking for him. They found him in a semi-conscious state in the vegetable garden and then dragged him to the house. As he was dragged to the house, the sniper fired at the members of his family that were carrying him away. They will give evidence that they saw spurts of dirt around their feet as they dragged [redacted] to the house. So in effect, it is one sniping incident resulting in a casualty, but it is two separate incidents in terms of there being sniping activity and more importantly, perhaps, the evidence that can be given by the daughter and cousin of the bullets hitting the dirt around their feet is strong evidence that the shooting of [redacted] in the first place was quite deliberate. They lived in a rural area just outside Sarajevo. There was no other dwelling within a space of something like 50 metres and no suggestion in the Prosecution case that there could have been someone in uniform or even someone not in uniform or who was a soldier nearby or any other legitimate military target. It therefore makes good sense to at least call two witnesses in that case. I should add that [redacted] was either unconscious or semi-conscious at that stage and he is not in a position to give evidence of the sniping activity as he was being dragged to the house. Your Honours, if you were to eliminate every one of the unscheduled sniping incident witnesses, again, the overall number of witnesses would be reduced by, I think, five. Those five being a particular individual who had the misfortune to be sniped and shelled, I think, five times. In other words, he was wounded five times in the indictment period on quite separate occasions. And the four witnesses who were initially intended for the first scheduled incident which has now become an unscheduled incident. In other words, almost without exception, the evidence of unscheduled sniping and shelling incidents comes from witnesses who were coming here anyway. But again, in response to Your Honours, could I propose this: In the 65 ter summaries, we have given particulars of the unscheduled shelling and sniping incidents. Your Honours will note that some of those incidents are very bare in terms of date, the identity of those wounded and so on. The point I think is well made without many of those incidents in the Prosecution case as to the scale and magnitude of the campaign which the Prosecution alleges. The Prosecution could eliminate a large number of those specific unscheduled shelling and sniping incidents so that when a witness entered the witness box, perhaps to give evidence of a scheduled sniping incident, instead of giving evidence of four other unscheduled sniping and shelling incidents, they give evidence of one or perhaps two. In other words, the -- in particular, the incidents for which there is available only the barest of details would be eliminated. And again the Prosecution's case in terms of evidence in chief would be significantly reduced. I'm making the point that it's very difficult to reduce these lists of primary categories and I'm also making the point that the way to reduce the Prosecution case is to eliminate some of the topics of evidence that each of these witnesses are giving. That still seems to me, Your Honours, to be the sensible approach in terms of solving the problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We were speaking about the number of witnesses mostly but it is also true that we need to address the question of the duration of the testimony because the question of shortening the case does not only depend on the number of witnesses, also on the quality of those witnesses and above all, on the time it takes for them to testify. There are a number of suggestions one could make, but of course it is not up to this Chamber to make any decisions regarding the future. We have to take decisions on the basis of the elements we have before us. I should now like to go on, or rather by way of introduction to a specific question, that is shelling incidents. I think that you have also indicated numerous expert witnesses on shelling. Does that -- do you have anything to add in relation to that such as the question of witnesses who had direct experience of those incidents and expert witnesses. So how do you view that, bearing in mind the need to economize?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour has observed that there are a large number of witnesses in relation to the shelling incidents, that is, the scheduled shelling incidents compared to the scheduled sniping incidents. The problem which I identified earlier with identifying the sniper applies equally to identifying those responsible for launching a shell. There are experts who are able to determine the direction and in some cases the distance from which a shell was fired and their testimony is essential, indeed critical to the Prosecution case in terms of proving that the origin of the shell for each of the five scheduled incidents was on the Sarajevo Romanija Corps side of the confrontation line. The origin of the shell, even at the time, was sometimes a matter of some controversy and in particular I have in mind the Markale shelling. There was an investigation carried out under the auspices of UNPROFOR to determine the origin of fire but there were some limitations placed on that investigation which in the Prosecution case were critical. It is necessary, in short, to have experts not only those experts, some of those experts who examined material at the time, but in some cases some additional experts to explain to the Trial Chamber the relevance of that earlier material. The Prosecution proposes to call a mortar expert, that is, a member of an armed force who has particular expertise in the area of mortars to explain to the Tribunal, to the Trial Chamber, to the extent it is necessary to understand these things, the basics of the operations of mortars, to explain to the Trial Chamber trajectories, the meaning of trajectories, issues to do with what is left in the crater when a mortar lands, and other aspects which ultimately the Trial Chamber will find very relevant to their task in relation to each of the scheduled incidents and some of the unscheduled incidents. Although the scheduled incidents all concern mortars, the campaign of shelling involved also the use of artillery, howitzers, tanks and the like, and it makes sense to have available, to include in the presentation of the Prosecution case an expert who can explain the limitations on the use of such weaponry, characteristics, and their capabilities, more importantly. A third expert who has been identified in the 65 ter material in relation to shelling is a ballistician. A ballistician is an expert who can from a background in physics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Ierace. We know that we have these experts on history, psychiatry, artillery, ballistics, arms and ammunition, superior responsibility, et cetera, et cetera, but I think this case is going to become a case for interdisciplinary discussions and that's a good thing, but I'm sorry for interrupting you, I would like to focus the discussion on something else, if possible. What we noted was the envisaged time for the testimony of these experts is frequently too long and the question would be: Would it be possible to shorten their testimony? What we have indicated already in a sense that expert witnesses file a report, the Defence will say whether yes or no they accept the report. If they agree with it, the report is admitted. I think it is under Rule 95(B) I think. If the Defence does not accept it, if it objects, then we have at least two possibilities. One is the one I've already mentioned, that is, the Defence can produce a counter-expertise. Not necessarily of the same length but to contradict the points that it objects to. And the Defence must say, "I don't accept," but that's not the end of it. The Defence also has it give its reasons, and the reasons are very important. And it has been the practice of this Chamber in other cases if a party would say that they do not accept a report, the party does -- which does not accept it has to give the reasons, and the Chamber would say to the party, "Yes. You have to 20 minutes to cross-examine expert witness on the points on which you disagree and the reasons why you disagree and object to the report." So we are discussing the possibility of shortening -- of reducing the number of witnesses but also shortening the duration of their testimony. Naturally, as I have said, there is the possibility of limiting the testimony of experts, to restricting it to the cross-examination for a fixed period of time because the Defence does not agree with certain conclusions reached, but the Defence always has the possibility, taking into account that the report is treated as the examination-in-chief. The Prosecutor files the report and that is the examination-in-chief. The Defence can cross-examine, and after that, the Prosecutor can re-examine. I think that that is absolutely fair. There's no prejudice to the rights of the Prosecution or the Defence in that way. So before hearing you, I think we have to have a short five-minute break. Perhaps you can stretch your legs, but it will only be for five minutes. --- Break taken at 5.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ierace, in relation to the question on the expert witnesses and the suggestions of the Trial Chamber to avoid the arrival of expert witnesses in order to shorten the testimony time, could you give us your opinion? And then I'll give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I give my opinion, I notice that the translation, both on the screen and orally, of Your Honours's words was to "avoid the arrival of expert witnesses." Would Your Honour clarify what you, in fact, said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would be pleased to do so. That's instead of having the witness come to the courtroom to testify only on the report or not to come at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the proposal that the report be the evidence in chief of a witness, is one which I enthusiastically embrace. The only additional material that the Prosecution would want to lead from the evidence that I can anticipate is evidence in relation to issues which had arisen perhaps during the course of the hearing before the report was prepared. However, I anticipate with some of the experts that may not, the tendering of the report as evidence in chief may not avoid them being present for the trial and giving evidence during the trial. There may still be some remaining issues which they are required to address, but certainly the proposal that their report be tendered would dramatically reduce their time in chief, and in some cases, I anticipate there would be no questions at all for the Prosecution to ask in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you didn't hear the question. The question that I asked the Prosecutor was to find a way of reducing the number of witnesses and the time of the testimony, because what I'm saying to the Prosecutor is going to be applicable as well to you, because if the Defence submits Defence expert reports, we'll do the same thing. If the Prosecutor doesn't accept a report the Prosecutor says why, and afterwards, he would have a specific amount of time in order to cross-examine the witness about the questions. And the same thing would apply to the Defence, which could ask additional question in respect to questions which you had raised. This is really a mirror imagine here. The rules that are established apply to both parties. And the questions that I had asked the Prosecutor, that is, where might it be possible to file the report, which would then be admitted, I think that's Rule 95 bis, or 94 bis it might be, but if one party does not accept the report, that party must say why it doesn't, and the party will be given a specific amount of time to cross-examine, and I say cross-examine, I repeat the word, the expert witness in respect of the reasons that the report was not accepted. There might be more complicated situations, or there is another possibility that one could file a counter-expertise on the points for which there is no agreement. I asked the Prosecutor to give us his opinion on that issue, and when doing so, I said I would ask the same question of the Defence and that's what I'm doing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was listening carefully to the submissions made by my learned colleague and to what you have just indicated. I have the Rule 94 bis in front of me, which provides that each party should file as soon as possible and not less than 21 days prior to the date on which the expert is expected to testify and so on and so forth. You're trying to have the parties behave as economically as possible in the proceedings. However, in view of the complexity of the case, as long as I have not received the reports and opinions of expert witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call, I am not in a position to present the submissions of the Defence in this respect. I do understand what the essence of your question is though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That's your answer, and you have the right to answer that way. But the question is almost one of principle, that is to see whether this way of proceeding is fair to both parties. It has nothing to do with a specific expert testimony. But you did give your opinion. That's your answer, and I take it as your answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now reached 92 bis witnesses. We have touched on that issue somewhat already. We know that the Defence has asked to cross-examine the ten witnesses, and we've already spoken about that. We are now turning to the Defence to find out whether it is maintaining this request and should we then conclude that the Defence is contesting all the exhibits with the depositions of those witnesses would tend -- would identify, that is, we could ask the question in more general terms. What are the reasons that you are contesting this type of testimony? Could you tell us that, please, Madam Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after we received the Prosecution brief including the proposal as to which witnesses need to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be heard, I have stated the problem that we have, that is, the time period that we had at our disposal and the possibility that we have had to familiarise ourselves with the summaries of witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call. As a preliminary matter, I have to state the following: You have indeed mentioned a very significant fact, namely that both the Defence and the Prosecution, during their joint work upon my suggestion as to the need to discuss the authenticity of the material -- and the Prosecution was required to make representations in -- pursuant to Rule 65 ter as to the authenticity of the material. So as regards this type of material, the parties have not discussed this particular issue during their contacts. As regards the brief of the Defence which I filed on the 4th of November, I was in a position to review the brief and to come to a conclusion as to which witnesses the Prosecutor intends to call, and in respect to which witnesses they intend to proceed pursuant to Rule 92 bis. By analysing the said Rule, we could see that no testimony is provided for, and any filing of the statements in accordance with Rule 92 bis, including the testimony about authenticity of statements, is something that we have stated in our brief. In particular, in point 4 of our brief, we stated that the witnesses that are identified in point 4 should testify about the acts and the behaviour of Mr. Galic, that of which he is charged. That is what I was able to conclude by reading the summaries of the witnesses put forward by the Prosecutor and I think that not even the statements from witnesses under point 4 cannot be used in this particular sense because we believe that these witnesses should be speaking, should be addressing the issue of the conduct of General Galic. Rule 92 bis provides for the possibility of testifying about the character of the accused, and in our view, these are two completely different interpretations. The Prosecutor is addressing the acts relating to the conduct of the accused and we believe that it's a very large topic and we don't think the matter should be addressed pursuant to Rule 92 bis and this is something that I emphasised in paragraph 5 of my brief. We have some problems with documentation during our work and my learned colleague has stated what the problem is with the medical documentation. In that sense, we made submissions in our brief, that is why we oppose that the statements of witnesses who will be called to testify to authenticate actually the documents pursuant to Rule 92. We actually want all of those witnesses to be called before the Chamber and subjected to cross-examination by the Defence; however, we intend to cross-examine them only in respect of the authenticity of the relevant documentation. In summary, as regards the essence of the Prosecution brief when it comes to the testimony of these witnesses, this is something that I am addressing in my brief and I want the Prosecutor to submit written statements in respect of witnesses who will be called to testify pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Pilipovic, I would like to be sure I understand. When you speak about contesting authenticity of the documents, if I could express myself that way, do you mean that the documents were completely fabricated or that the documents did not really respect the usual procedure? Could you tell us what kind of objections you would have in respect of authenticity of documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will tell you right away. The medical documentation was submitted to the Defence in a completely illegible form. From the medical documentation that was provided to the Defence, we cannot see when the injury of the relevant person in respect of whom the document is provided occurred. We cannot even read the name and the surname of the person or the time of the incident or the description of the injury and I am referring to all of these medical documents. My colleagues are aware of this problem and it is probably because of those -- out of those reasons that they obtained statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis and it is in that manner that they seek to prove the authenticity of the medical documentation. Second, as regards the maps that I received from my learned friends from the Prosecution, we dispute their authenticity because from a simple review of such maps, one can conclude that they are not from the relevant times from the period of time which is covered in the indictment which concerns the accused, General Galic. At this point in time and I have already stated that I received the relevant brief together with the attachments on the 6th of November, I cannot say which of the documents should be relevant in this respect. I haven't been able to analyse them all, but at this point in time, my position, Your Honour, is that the Defence disputes the authenticity of the documents; however, we did not address those documents individually together with my colleagues from the Prosecution. Had we been able to address this particular issue, I think the problem would have been less serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are at least two questions here. One is to know whether you have any originals for which you could make legible copies? Mrs. Pilipovic is saying they cannot read the documents because of the quality of the photocopies, they can't read the dates. What she is saying is that she doesn't have a document, really, that she can contest. It's not really a question of authenticity but rather one of legibility of documents. The other aspect is one of authenticity in respect of the maps. Would you like to add something about that, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a gross overstatement to say that these documents are illegible as to names and dates and particular incidents. It is in fact the case that they are basically legible. There are occasionally some words which are illegible. I don't know whether my friend intended it, but going on the translation that I've read, the impression conveyed is that they are all illegible and it's far from that. In relation to the maps, I think my friend is referring to a proposed 92 bis statement to the effect that certain maps which the Prosecution proposes to tender come from archives of the -- particular archives and that's the purpose for which the Prosecution seeks a 92 bis statement in relation to the maps. So again, there seems to be perhaps some misunderstanding on the part of the Prosecution's intention. Your Honour has asked me directly whether we have the original medical records. They are with the different hospitals in Sarajevo and we -- the Prosecution has recently arranged for an investigator to return to those hospitals and to obtain, where possible, better copies or additional documents. All of that product will be -- excuse me, Your Honour, was disclosed on the 26th of October, a week or so after we obtained it in Sarajevo. They are the best copies that we can get. And as I said earlier, where there is occasionally a word or a sentence that is not entirely legible, then the usual approach applies. The Prosecution produces evidence, tenders evidence and it's a matter of whether the Prosecution has made out its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can conclude then that the Prosecutor has an advantage in respect of reading as compared to the Defence because the Prosecutor has been able to read an understand the documents; is that what I should take from what you said, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution has also been unable to read some words in the documentation. The point I'm making is that it is a minor problem, it is not a major problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In any case, the question about the legibility is important because it means that if the Defence is unable to read the document, it would therefore contest it and a witness cannot be heard under 92 bis and that's very important. I think this is a question that the parties have got to resolve together, at least meet, and they could assist one another in order to reach a conclusion. Can we read what we have or could we get better copies. But the question of legibility is very important and I think the parties have to do that work because the Chamber does not have the document and therefore is not in the position to help you. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me very briefly to say a few things about this question of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter, Rule 65 ter, is the -- M, particularly paragraph M is what I'm referring to, the Defence has to receive the documents that you are speaking about and there is an imperative obligation on the Prosecution to submit to the Defence within six weeks, that is a time period which cannot be changed. I had checked with the assistance of your Registry and apparently it appears that that time limit was not respected. When the framework for this trial was set up, that is, when the rules are not respected and are not respected is a problem and when we look under that same rule, sections M and N, I remind you that your Chamber has the power to say that under those circumstances, further to the report to the pre-trial judge, that you simply do not accept some or all of the documents or materials that were submitted by the Prosecutor outside the delay of the time period of six weeks. One of the greatest, the most important interests of justice is not, as you said, is not to waste time or money of the International Community and since the sanctions were provided for in cases which have arisen as today, these have got to be recognised and it has to do with the very principle of the fairness of the trial, and I believe that you were saying that yourself, Your Honour. But we have got an excellent way, it seems to me, to shorten the discussions and a great deal of the trial by applying the solution which has been -- which is applied by Rule 65 ter (N) these words, "the sanctions can be imposed on a party." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Perhaps we can stay another two or three minutes to finish with the issue of the witnesses and we'll wait until tomorrow to deal with the exhibits list. Tomorrow, we can check on the deadline questions, and if the trial can't open on the 3rd of December well, then, it can start on the 6th or the 7th. That would not be a problem. The last question regarding the witness list is the specific case of video conferences. In my mind, I am thinking about three witnesses by video conference, but I have a question about a fourth -- the fourth one. As regards those witnesses that would be asked to testify by video conference or videolink, it seems it might be better to wait until the Chamber hearing the case to choose the moment it judges appropriate to take a decision. But right now we would like to know from the Prosecutor what the reasons are that these witnesses will be presented by videolink to the Chamber because I think these -- we don't have circumstances or reasons that would bring the Prosecutor to using videolinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a number of the witnesses in Sarajevo who could be described as crime-based witnesses such as victims of shelling or sniping in the Prosecution case are in poor health and are not able, because of poor health, to travel to The Hague or have other pressing reasons as to why, in my submission, they should give their evidence by videolink from Sarajevo, such as family responsibilities or age, extreme age. That is the nature of the reasoning behind that request that a number of those witnesses give their evidence in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your way of thinking, Mr. Ierace -- well, let me start again. Reasoning, as we have been doing, that the Chamber wants to shorten things and you want to keep things as they are, for your case, are these witnesses really essential?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps I could make a proposal in relation to the concern that you have expressed. Your Honour has said that you intend to sit tomorrow, and my friends have said that they have only had the benefit of 48 hours to consider the material. Could I respectfully suggest that if Your Honour was able to continue the hearing, subject to my friends' timetable on, say, Monday, that would give them an additional precious few days to look at the material and in the meantime, I could review the witness list with a view to shortening the number of witnesses. Because so many witnesses give evidence of more than one critical area is not a function that is easily done. If one reduces a witness because of testimony in one area, there may be implications in a number of others. I make the proposal because it seems to me that within the space of a few days, we may be able to significantly reduce it, and keeping in mind some comments made by Your Honour during the course of this afternoon. So I propose that to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Pilipovic, would you agree to that suggestion or do you have another suggestion? Would you prefer to sit tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you're asking me, Your Honour, although three days are not going to make much difference, I think I will be much more useful on Monday. It would suit us better on Monday,, and at least I will have an opportunity to review in detail the relevant documents and the brief, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but as you are to take a decision like that is complicated. Complicated, because you know that the courtrooms are very busy so one has to find a slot in order to be able to do that. So I was just told about the courtrooms that we can sit on Monday in the afternoon. If, Madam Pilipovic, that is not useful to you, it might be more -- it might be somewhat useful. But the essential issue here as I've said from the very beginning is that we're now dealing with the Prosecutor's pre-trial matters, and we've got to have all the information to give the Prosecutor to make the efforts to shorten the witness list. As I said, you will be in the same situation because when we get to the Defence pre-trial case, you will have the opportunity to go through this exercise as well. In any case, Mr. Ierace, excuse me for saying that to you. Mr. Ierace, I think that you are sincerely trying to shorten the witness list. What I can tell you is that our intention, that is, the intention of the Chamber, is either to reduce the number of witnesses or perhaps give to you a specific amount of time that you can do what you want with. In principle, we have about 60 days, that is, either you drop the number of witnesses in order to fit into that 60-day figure in order to present your case and then fine, or the Chamber can tell you, "Mr. Prosecutor, you have 60 days to present your case", and the number of days given to the Prosecution out of a sense of fairness would be given to the Defence. That's the direction the Chamber is going to take. That's what we have in mind, but we'll see what the results are, Mr. Ierace. In any case, we're beginning to have some experience in cases here at the Tribunal, and we know that we can -- that we can present the case, even a case of this size, within a 60-day period for hearing. As I said, those are the limits, either you think about a specific time or you think about shortening the number of witnesses on the list. Did you want to add something, Mr. Ierace? But we've got to end our session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour please clarify whether that 60-day period includes the opening and, more particularly, the proposed visit by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Trial Chamber to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the commencement of the trial, I'm not sure what you are talking about, but the commencement of the trial will be short because we've got the pre-trial briefs so it's not going to take more than the morning, at least I don't think so. That's my thought. Those days do not include the possible visit to Sarajevo. We still haven't taken a decision on that question but I'm speaking about the 60 days for presenting the case in the courtroom, and in those days I include the opening statement because I think that it should not go on for more than a morning. We've got the pre-trial briefs and almost everything is in them. If there is nothing else to say today, we are going to meet again here on Monday in the afternoon at 2.30. I wish you a good weekend for those people going to work, good work. A correction need to be made, in courtroom number 3 and not here. When he said here, I was actually referring to the Tribunal. 6.14 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday the 12th day of November, 2001, at 2.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.14 p.m.,
